turns.player: Greet Sister Vreni warmly and hear her out fully before deciding anything
turns.summary: Sister Vreni arrived at Mara's garden gate seeking the healer who closed a traveler's wound; she extended a warm, plain invitation to serve at the pass-road wayhouse, which has no resident healer since the equinox.
turns.narration:
The evening light has gone amber and low over Mara's back garden, the seedling beds throwing long shadows across the path. You turn toward the gate where Sister Vreni stands — the pale gray habit, the folded hands, the patient quality of someone who has learned to wait without pressing.

"Sister," you say, and the warmth in it is genuine. "Please — come in, if you like. Or I can come to you."

She does not move from the gate, which is itself a kind of courtesy — she will not enter uninvited — but she unfolds her hands and lets something ease in her face. "I came to find the healer who closed a wound on a traveler who arrived eleven days ago. A thigh wound, carefully cleaned. It closed without trouble." A brief pause, measuring. "That is not common in wayhouse work. We notice when something is done well."

She tells you the rest plainly: the wayhouse above the pass road has no healer resident at present. The woman who kept that post through the summer returned to her family at the equinox. The sisters manage, but managing is not the same as knowing, and there are people on the road who need more than bandage linen and the will to apply it. The invitation is warm and direct — come and stay a while, help as you're able, see whether it suits.

Aevi drifts closer to your shoulder as Sister Vreni finishes, her motes brightening just a degree — the quiet attention she reserves for things she finds worth watching. Behind you, Mara has gone still in the way she does when she is listening and not yet deciding whether to speak.

turns.player: Accept the invitation openly — you are a healer and this is a place that needs one; tell her you will come and ask when she needs you
turns.summary: Adelheid accepted Sister Vreni's invitation to the pass-road wayhouse; Vreni named it as a stop on the sluice-road above the Wet Meadows — the road Silas Weir would have traveled three weeks ago.
turns.narration:
The amber light holds a moment longer as you step toward the gate. 'I'll come,' you tell Sister Vreni, and mean it simply — no hesitation, no performance of weighing it. 'I am a healer, and you have need of one. That is enough.'

Something settles in her face. Not relief exactly — more the quality of someone who prepared for a longer conversation and finds they do not need it. 'The wayhouse would have you as soon as you are ready. There is no fixed date. We see travelers throughout the week, and the room has been empty since the equinox.' She pauses. 'A woman came down the pass road two days ago with her youngest — a fever running four days. We managed, but it was close. Another pair of hands with real knowledge would have changed that morning.'

Behind you, Mara makes a small sound — not quite approval, not quite disagreement. Something more like: she is noting this. When you glance back she is standing with arms folded, watching the two of you with the particular stillness of someone who already saw this coming and is now deciding what it means for her own ledger.

'The wayhouse sits on the sluice-road,' Sister Vreni adds quietly, as if it is simply geography. 'Above the Wet Meadows. Travelers heading upstream pass through — we know most of them by the third week of a season.' She does not say Silas Weir's name. She does not need to. The wayhouse would have seen him, three weeks ago, heading toward the sluice-turn. She is offering you both a posting and a vantage point, and doing it with complete honesty about what the wayhouse is. Aevi drifts close to your ear, her motes brightening to a pleased teal. 'A healer at the crossroads of the sluice-road,' she murmurs. 'That is a useful place to be.'

Mara's voice comes from behind you, dry and unhurried: 'When will you go, then?'

turns.player: Ask Mara directly what she thinks of this — she saw it coming; you want her read before you commit to the road
turns.summary: Adelheid asked Mara directly for her read on the wayhouse invitation; Mara gave it plain — the road upstream needs someone with a reason to be on it. Aevi noted the distinction.
turns.narration:
The question turns you back toward Mara before Sister Vreni can fill the silence further. She is still at the step, arms folded, watching — not disapproving, not approving. Waiting, the way she waits for ledger columns to add themselves up.

"What do you think?" you ask her directly. "You saw her coming before I did. You see most things before anyone else does."

A beat. Mara unfolds her arms, slowly, and lets them settle at her sides. It is the closest thing to relaxing you have seen from her.

"I think," she says, "that the wayhouse is on the sluice-road." She says it the way she might say the accounts balance — plain, final, not an argument. "I think Sister Vreni would not have come this far for a closed wound if the wayhouse did not need someone. And I think—" a pause, shorter than the first — "that the road upstream is going to need someone on it who has a reason to be there."

She is not telling you to go. She is telling you that going is a sound decision, and from Mara Wells that is the same thing as a blessing.

Aevi drifts close to your ear, a small warm brightening. "She said the road upstream," the motes murmur, barely audible. "Not the wayhouse. The road."

Sister Vreni has the grace to look at the seedling beds during this.

turns.player: Ask Sister Vreni how soon she is heading back — and whether you might walk the first stretch of the road together tonight.
turns.summary: Adelheid asked Sister Vreni about her departure and received an open invitation to walk the sluice-road to the wayhouse together tonight by moonlight.
turns.narration:
The question comes out easily, no ceremony in it. "When are you heading back, Sister? Tonight, or do you wait for morning?"

Sister Vreni turns from the seedling beds, where she has been studying something low in the soil with the quiet attention of a person who notices growing things. "Tonight," she says. "I came down on foot this afternoon. The road is sound enough by moonlight and I know the first stretch well." A small pause. "You are welcome to walk it with me, if you are ready. The wayhouse is not far — an hour and a half, perhaps two if the dew has come early and made the stones slippery."

Mara says nothing from her step, but there is a quality in her silence that is not absence — she is listening, noting, committing something to her internal ledger. When you glance back at her she gives you a look that is almost a nod. Almost.

Aevi brightens slightly at your shoulder — not alarm, just attention. The motes rearrange into a loose question-mark shape, which is her way of asking whether you want to talk through what you are carrying before you go. *The cutting is wrapped,* she murmurs, just inside your ear. *The satchel is stocked. You are as ready as the road asks.* She dims back to her usual slow drift, content to let you decide.

There is nothing holding you here in the garden but the garden itself — the cool evening breath, the seedling beds, the last of the amber draining from the sky. Tomorrow's tasks will not start tonight. The road, though, starts now.

personalArc.name: The Root Remembers
personalArc.premise: A Swiss herbalist transplanted to an alien soil carries a silver-stemmed cutting from her village — the last living thread to everything she understood — and must decide whether her knowledge is a heritage to preserve or a seed to break open and replant entirely, in ground that does not know her name.
personalArc.stakes: To remain the keeper of a dead village's remedies, or to become something that village never imagined: a healer fluent in two earths, whose hands hold the old world and the new one at once — or to lose both trying.

legendNpc.name: The Silver-Stemmed Cutting
legendNpc.role: the last living root of her Swiss village, wrapped in linen and slowly dying, the mute accusation of every mile she was

stages.objective: the cutting that will not root — she has tried three times; the Korean soil rejects it, or she does not yet know how to ask; Mara Wells has seen this particular grief before, in other hands, and says so plainly

the remedy that should not work — she compounds a draught from Korean plants she only half-understands, borrowing Piotr's hard-won field notes, and it heals something her Swiss formulary swore was untreatable; the success feels like a betrayal, and a door

the linen unwrapped — the cutting is failing; she must choose what she owes it, what she owes Millbrook, and what she owes the healer she is becoming; the answer is in what she does with the roots when she finally opens the wrapping and faces what is left

personalArc.notes_for_gm: A generated PERSONAL arc (SNG-133) — surface it as a slow gravity across sessions; the ending is the player's, never foreclosed.
